prompt: Which of the following best describes demand for a good?

options.label: A
options.text: The quantities consumers are willing and able to purchase at different prices

options.label: B
options.text: The satisfaction consumers receive from the last unit purchased

options.label: C
options.text: The income consumers have available after purchasing the good

options.label: D
options.text: The number of consumers who are legally permitted to buy the good

options.label: E
options.text: The quantity consumers purchase at one price during a given period

explanation: Demand lists how much consumers are willing and able to buy at each possible price.

prompt: The law of demand states that, other things constant,

options.label: A
options.text: Demand decreases whenever consumers' nominal income increases

options.label: B
options.text: Demand increases whenever the number of consumers decreases

options.label: C
options.text: Quantity demanded remains constant when the good's price changes

options.label: D
options.text: Quantity demanded decreases when the good's own price increases

options.label: E
options.text: Quantity demanded increases when the good's own price increases

explanation: With other factors held constant, a higher price makes consumers willing to buy fewer units. This inverse relationship is the law of demand.

prompt: If the price of a good decreases, which of the following will most likely occur, ceteris paribus?

options.label: A
options.text: The quantity demanded of the good will decrease

options.label: B
options.text: The quantity demanded of the good will remain unchanged

options.label: C
options.text: The quantity demanded of the good will increase

options.label: D
options.text: The demand for the good will shift to the left

options.label: E
options.text: The demand for the good will shift to the right

explanation: A lower price encourages consumers to buy more units. This is movement down the existing demand curve.

prompt: Which of the following is a determinant that can shift the demand curve for a good?

options.label: A
options.text: The slope measured between two points on the curve

options.label: B
options.text: Consumers' expectations about the good's future price

options.label: C
options.text: The good's current price, with other factors constant

options.label: D
options.text: The price-quantity combination selected on the curve

options.label: E
options.text: The quantity currently shown on the demand curve

explanation: Expected future prices affect when consumers choose to buy. A change in expectations can therefore shift current demand at every price.

prompt: A downward-sloping demand curve shows that

options.label: A
options.text: Higher expected prices are associated with smaller current demand

options.label: B
options.text: Lower prices are associated with larger quantities demanded

options.label: C
options.text: Lower prices are associated with smaller quantities demanded

options.label: D
options.text: More buyers are associated with smaller market demand

options.label: E
options.text: Higher incomes are associated with larger quantities demanded

explanation: A downward-sloping curve pairs lower prices with larger quantities demanded, holding other demand determinants constant.

prompt: Based on the figure below, which labeled point represents the larger quantity demanded?

options.label: A
options.text: Neither point, because both lie on the same demand curve

options.label: B
options.text: Point B, because it is associated with the lower price

options.label: C
options.text: Point A, because it is farther from the quantity axis

options.label: D
options.text: Point A, because it is associated with the higher price

options.label: E
options.text: Point B, because it represents a rightward demand shift

explanation: Point B has a lower price and a larger quantity than point A. Both points lie on the same demand curve.
graphDescription: Price is on the vertical axis and quantity demanded is on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping curve labeled D contains point A at a high price and low quantity and point B at a lower price and larger quantity.

prompt: A change in a good's own price causes

options.label: A
options.text: A rightward shift of its demand curve at every price

options.label: B
options.text: A change in consumer preferences for the good

options.label: C
options.text: Movement along the demand curve

options.label: D
options.text: A change in the number of buyers in its market

options.label: E
options.text: A leftward shift of its demand curve at every price

explanation: Changing the good's own price changes the quantity consumers choose on the existing demand curve.

prompt: An increase in demand for a good means that consumers

options.label: A
options.text: Buy more at each possible price

options.label: B
options.text: Buy more only because the good's current price has fallen

options.label: C
options.text: Move upward and leftward along the existing demand curve

options.label: D
options.text: Face a smaller quantity range on the existing demand schedule

options.label: E
options.text: Are willing to buy less at every possible price

explanation: When demand increases, consumers are willing and able to buy more at each price. The demand curve shifts right.

prompt: For a normal good, an increase in consumer income will most likely

options.label: A
options.text: Decrease demand for the good

options.label: B
options.text: Increase demand for the good

options.label: C
options.text: Decrease quantity demanded by raising its price

options.label: D
options.text: Leave demand unchanged at every price

options.label: E
options.text: Increase quantity demanded by lowering its price

explanation: Consumers buy more of a normal good at each price when their income rises, shifting demand right.

prompt: Based on the figure below, the change from point A to point B is best described as

options.label: A
options.text: A decrease in quantity demanded caused by a lower price

options.label: B
options.text: Higher quantity demanded after a price decrease

options.label: C
options.text: A decrease in demand caused by weaker preferences

options.label: D
options.text: An increase in demand caused by more consumers

options.label: E
options.text: An increase in demand caused by an increase in income

explanation: The move to B lowers price and raises quantity on D1. It therefore represents an increase in quantity demanded.
graphDescription: Price is on the vertical axis and quantity demanded is on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping curve labeled D1 contains point A at price P1 and quantity Q1 and point B at lower price P2 and larger quantity Q2. An arrow points from A to B.

graphScenes.caption: Schematic; only labeled numbers are quantitative

prompt: For an inferior good, an increase in consumer income will most likely

options.label: A
options.text: Increase quantity demanded along the same curve

options.label: B
options.text: Decrease demand for the good

options.label: C
options.text: Increase demand for the good

options.label: D
options.text: Leave demand unchanged because income is not a price

options.label: E
options.text: Decrease quantity demanded along the same curve

explanation: An inferior good is one consumers buy less of as income rises. Higher income shifts its demand curve left.

prompt: If tea and coffee are substitutes, an increase in the price of tea will most likely

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the quantity demanded of coffee along its curve

options.label: B
options.text: Decrease the demand for coffee

options.label: C
options.text: Decrease the quantity demanded of coffee along its curve

options.label: D
options.text: Increase the demand for coffee

options.label: E
options.text: Leave the demand for coffee unchanged at every price

explanation: A higher tea price makes coffee a more attractive substitute. Consumers demand more coffee at each coffee price.

prompt: If printers and ink cartridges are complements, a decrease in the price of printers will most likely

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the demand for ink cartridges

options.label: B
options.text: Leave the demand for ink cartridges unchanged at every price

options.label: C
options.text: Decrease the quantity demanded of ink cartridges along its curve

options.label: D
options.text: Decrease the demand for ink cartridges

options.label: E
options.text: Increase the quantity demanded of ink cartridges along its curve

explanation: Cheaper printers encourage printer purchases. Since ink is used with printers, demand for ink cartridges increases.

prompt: Based on the figure below, which of the following could have caused the shift from D1 to D2 for a normal good?

options.label: A
options.text: An increase in consumer income

options.label: B
options.text: An increase in the good's current price

options.label: C
options.text: A decrease in consumer income

options.label: D
options.text: A decrease in the number of consumers

options.label: E
options.text: A decrease in the good's current price

explanation: The rightward shift to D2 shows greater demand at each price. Higher income produces this change for a normal good.

prompt: An increase in consumers' preference for a good will most likely

options.label: A
options.text: Shift the demand curve for the good to the right

options.label: B
options.text: Shift the demand curve for the good to the left

options.label: C
options.text: Leave the demand curve in its original position

options.label: D
options.text: Cause movement downward along the demand curve

options.label: E
options.text: Cause movement upward along the demand curve

explanation: A stronger preference makes consumers willing to buy more at the same prices, shifting demand right.

prompt: An increase in the number of buyers in a market will most likely

options.label: A
options.text: Increase quantity demanded on one consumer's curve

options.label: B
options.text: Decrease market demand at each price

options.label: C
options.text: Leave market demand unchanged at each price

options.label: D
options.text: Increase market demand at each price

options.label: E
options.text: Decrease quantity demanded on one consumer's curve

explanation: Adding buyers adds their purchases to the market total at each price. Market demand therefore increases.

prompt: If consumers expect a good's price to rise next month, its current demand will most likely

options.label: A
options.text: Remain unchanged because the expected price is not current

options.label: B
options.text: Decrease as some purchases are moved to the future

options.label: C
options.text: Increase only after the current price has decreased

options.label: D
options.text: Decrease only after the current price has increased

options.label: E
options.text: Increase as some purchases are moved to the present

explanation: Consumers expecting a higher future price may buy now to avoid paying more later. This increases current demand.

prompt: Based on the figure below, which of the following is consistent with the shift shown for bus rides?

options.label: A
options.text: An increase in the number of people who regularly commute

options.label: B
options.text: An increase in the current price of a bus ride

options.label: C
options.text: An increase in preference for public transportation

options.label: D
options.text: A decrease in the number of people who regularly commute

options.label: E
options.text: A decrease in the current price of a bus ride

explanation: Fewer commuters mean fewer potential buyers of bus rides. This reduces demand and shifts the curve left.
graphDescription: Price per bus ride is on the vertical axis and quantity of bus rides demanded is on the horizontal axis. Two downward-sloping curves are labeled D1 and D2, with D2 entirely to the left of D1. An arrow points from D1 toward D2.

prompt: The market demand curve for a good is found by

options.label: A
options.text: Selecting the individual demand curve with the most purchases

options.label: B
options.text: Subtracting the smallest individual demand from the largest

options.label: C
options.text: Adding the prices each consumer pays at each quantity

options.label: D
options.text: Averaging individual quantities demanded at each price

options.label: E
options.text: Adding individual quantities demanded at each price

explanation: At any given price, add the quantities demanded by all buyers. Repeating this across prices produces market demand.

prompt: At a price of $8, Ana demands 3 units and Ben demands 5 units. If they are the only buyers, market quantity demanded is

options.label: A
options.text: 5 units

options.label: B
options.text: 8 units

options.label: C
options.text: 15 units

options.label: D
options.text: 3 units

options.label: E
options.text: 2 units

explanation: Both buyers face the same $8 price, so their quantities add to 3 + 5 = 8 units.

prompt: Why are well-defined property rights important for a market system?

options.label: A
options.text: They require every good to have the same demand curve

options.label: B
options.text: They ensure every consumer assigns the same value to property

options.label: C
options.text: They prevent consumer preferences from changing over time

options.label: D
options.text: They clarify who may use, exchange, and benefit from property

options.label: E
options.text: They make every buyer face the same income constraint

explanation: Property rights identify who controls an asset and can transfer it. Buyers and sellers can exchange more confidently when these rights are clear.

prompt: A consumer who wants a concert ticket but cannot afford it is primarily facing

options.label: A
options.text: A substitution effect

options.label: B
options.text: A market-demand calculation

options.label: C
options.text: A change in tastes

options.label: D
options.text: A diminishing-utility schedule

options.label: E
options.text: An income constraint

explanation: The consumer's income limits what they can afford. Without enough money for the ticket, the desired purchase is outside that budget.

prompt: A commuter chooses a nearby grocery store because only 20 minutes are available to shop. This decision best illustrates

options.label: A
options.text: A substitution effect caused by relative prices

options.label: B
options.text: A movement along a market demand curve

options.label: C
options.text: A change in market demand caused by more buyers

options.label: D
options.text: An income effect caused by a price change

options.label: E
options.text: A time constraint affecting consumer choice

explanation: Only stores reachable within the available 20 minutes are practical options. The time constraint therefore affects the commuter's choice.

prompt: Based on the figure below, a decrease in the good's price from P1 to P2 causes

options.label: A
options.text: Quantity demanded to increase from Q1 to Q2

options.label: B
options.text: Demand to decrease along the same curve

options.text: Quantity demanded to decrease from Q2 to Q1

options.label: D
options.text: Demand to increase from D1 to D2

options.label: E
options.text: The number of buyers to increase automatically

explanation: Moving from P1 to the lower P2 on D1 raises quantity demanded from Q1 to Q2.

prompt: Diminishing marginal utility helps explain the downward slope of demand because

options.label: A
options.text: Additional units generally provide more extra satisfaction, so buyers accept higher prices

options.label: B
options.text: Lower incomes generally increase purchasing power, so buyers purchase more units

options.label: C
options.text: Additional units generally provide less extra satisfaction, so buyers require lower prices

options.label: D
options.text: Additional buyers generally reduce market demand, so each consumer purchases fewer units

options.label: E
options.text: Higher expected prices generally reduce current purchases, so buyers postpone consumption

explanation: Successive units usually provide less additional satisfaction. Consumers consequently need a lower price to make buying those extra units worthwhile.

prompt: The substitution effect of a decrease in a good's price predicts that consumers will

options.label: A
options.text: Demand less of every alternative because their money income has fallen

options.label: B
options.text: Purchase more of the good because it is cheaper relative to alternatives

options.label: C
options.text: Purchase less of the good because it is cheaper relative to alternatives

options.label: D
options.text: Shift the good's demand curve right because its own price is lower

options.label: E
options.text: Shift the good's demand curve left because its own price is lower

explanation: The price decrease makes the good cheaper relative to alternatives. Consumers substitute toward it and buy more.

prompt: The income effect of a decrease in a good's price occurs because the lower price

options.label: A
options.text: Increases the consumer's nominal income by the price change

options.label: B
options.text: Decreases the purchasing power of the consumer's income

options.label: C
options.text: Increases the number of buyers included in market demand

options.label: D
options.text: Increases the purchasing power of the consumer's income

options.label: E
options.text: Decreases the number of alternatives available to the consumer

explanation: A lower price lets the same income buy more goods and services. The resulting increase in real purchasing power creates the income effect.

prompt: A demand curve may also be interpreted as a marginal benefit curve because it shows

options.label: A
options.text: The number of consumers willing to enter the market at each price

options.label: B
options.text: The minimum income consumers need to purchase every available unit

options.label: C
options.text: The total satisfaction consumers receive from all units purchased

options.label: D
options.text: The change in purchasing power created by each additional buyer

options.label: E
options.text: The maximum price consumers are willing to pay for each additional unit

explanation: Willingness to pay for one additional unit measures its marginal benefit. A demand curve shows these values for successive units.

prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes demand from quantity demanded?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand is an amount at one price; quantity demanded is the full price-quantity relationship

options.label: B
options.text: Demand applies to individuals; quantity demanded applies only to an entire market

options.label: C
options.text: Demand is the full price-quantity relationship; quantity demanded is an amount at one price

options.label: D
options.text: Demand changes only with own-price; quantity demanded changes only with consumer income

options.label: E
options.text: Demand measures willingness to buy; quantity demanded measures willingness without ability

explanation: Demand is the complete relationship between prices and purchases. Quantity demanded is the amount consumers choose at one particular price.

prompt: A law prohibiting minors from purchasing a particular product primarily changes their consumer decisions by imposing

options.label: A
options.text: Diminishing marginal utility

options.label: B
options.text: A legal constraint

options.label: C
options.text: A substitution effect

options.label: D
options.text: An income effect

options.label: E
options.text: A market-demand summation

explanation: The prohibition makes the purchase legally unavailable to minors. It therefore limits their feasible choices through a legal constraint.

prompt: Based on the figure below, which combination of events is represented by the movement from A to B and the shift from D1 to D2?

options.label: A
options.text: A decrease in the good's price, followed by an increase in consumer preference

options.label: E
options.text: An increase in the good's price, followed by a decrease in consumer preference

prompt: Household incomes increase, and purchases of restaurant meals rise at every listed price. Which conclusion is best supported?

prompt: A worker receives a raise and purchases fewer instant noodles at every price. The worker's demand behavior indicates that instant noodles are

explanation: The worker demands fewer noodles after the raise. This negative income-demand relationship makes noodles an inferior good for that worker.

prompt: Movie tickets and streaming subscriptions are substitutes. If streaming subscription prices decrease, which of the following will most likely occur?

options.label: B
options.text: Demand for movie tickets will decrease at every ticket price

options.text: Demand for movie tickets will remain unchanged at every ticket price

options.text: Quantity demanded of movie tickets will decrease along its curve

prompt: If smartphones and protective cases are complements, an increase in the price of smartphones will most likely

prompt: Consumers expect laptop prices to fall substantially next month. Which of the following will most likely occur in the current month?

prompt: At a price of $12, three consumers demand 2, 4, and 5 units, respectively. At a price of $10, they demand 3, 5, and 7 units. Which pair gives market quantity demanded at the two prices?

prompt: A consumer chooses a more expensive nearby pharmacy rather than a distant discount pharmacy because medication is needed immediately. Which factor best explains the choice?

prompt: A city requires a permit before residents may purchase a restricted chemical. Holding prices constant, the requirement will most directly

prompt: Secure ownership records make buyers more willing to purchase used bicycles because buyers can verify that sellers may legally transfer them. This outcome best illustrates how property rights

options.text: Increase demand by raising every buyer's money income

prompt: Demand for a normal good will unambiguously increase if consumer income rises and

options.label: A
options.text: The price of a substitute also rises

options.label: B
options.text: The number of buyers decreases

options.label: C
options.text: The price of a substitute decreases

options.label: D
options.text: Consumers expect a lower future price

options.label: E

prompt: Based on the figure below, which statement best explains why demand moved from D1 to D2 despite an increase in consumer income for this normal good?

options.label: A
options.text: The income increase reduced demand because the good must be normal

options.label: B
options.text: Another determinant reduced demand by more than the income increase raised it

options.label: C
options.text: Another determinant raised demand by more than the income increase did

options.label: D
options.text: The good's current price increased and shifted demand from D1 to D2

options.label: E
options.text: The income increase caused movement upward along D1 instead of a shift

explanation: Higher income pushes a normal good's demand right, yet the graph shows a leftward shift. Another demand-reducing change must have outweighed the income effect.
graphDescription: Price is on the vertical axis and quantity demanded is on the horizontal axis. Demand shifts left from D1 to D2. A note states that consumer income increased and the good is normal, while the graph shows the net change after all determinants changed.

prompt: The price of a normal good decreases at the same time consumer income increases. Which statement correctly describes the two effects?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand shifts left while quantity demanded increases along the original curve

options.label: B
options.text: Quantity demanded increases twice along the original demand curve

options.label: C
options.text: Quantity demanded increases along a demand curve, and the demand curve shifts right

options.label: D
options.text: Quantity demanded decreases along a demand curve, and the demand curve shifts left

options.label: E
options.text: Demand shifts right twice because both changes are demand determinants

explanation: The price decrease raises quantity demanded along the curve. The income increase separately shifts demand right because the good is normal.

prompt: Consumer income rises for a normal good while the good's own price remains unchanged. The resulting increase in purchases is best described as

options.label: A
options.text: A decrease in demand measured at the unchanged price

options.label: B
options.text: An increase in demand measured at the unchanged price

options.label: C
options.text: A movement along the original curve caused by higher income

options.label: D
options.text: A decrease in quantity demanded caused by a higher own-price

options.label: E
options.text: An increase in quantity demanded caused by a lower own-price

explanation: Income changes the quantity consumers want at every price. Purchases rise at the unchanged price because the normal good's demand shifts right.

prompt: The price of Good X decreases while the price of its substitute, Good Y, increases. Which statement about Good X is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Both changes increase the quantity of Good X purchased, but through different mechanisms

options.label: B
options.text: The effects necessarily offset because one changes price and the other changes demand

options.label: C
options.text: The lower price of X shifts its demand right, while the higher price of Y causes movement

options.label: D
options.text: The lower price of X causes movement, while the higher price of Y shifts demand left

options.label: E
options.text: Both changes decrease the quantity of Good X purchased through the same mechanism

explanation: X's lower price increases purchases along its demand curve. Y's higher price makes X more attractive as a substitute and shifts X's demand right.

prompt: Consumers expect the price of game consoles to rise next month while the current price of complementary games increases. What is the effect on current demand for consoles?

options.label: A
options.text: It remains unchanged because neither change is the console's current price

options.label: B
options.text: Current console demand will increase because both changes make current console purchases relatively more attractive

options.label: C
options.text: It increases because the game-price increase causes movement down the console demand curve

options.label: D
options.text: It decreases because both changes make current console purchases less attractive

options.label: E
options.text: It is indeterminate because the expectation raises demand while the game-price increase lowers it

explanation: Expected higher console prices encourage buying now, while more expensive complementary games discourage console purchases. The net effect depends on which change is larger.

prompt: Based on the figure below, which sequence is represented by the change from A to B and then from B to C?

options.label: A
options.text: A decrease in demand followed by an increase in the good's own price

options.label: B
options.text: An increase in demand followed by a decrease in the good's own price

options.label: C
options.text: An increase in the good's own price followed by an increase in demand

options.label: D
options.text: An increase in quantity demanded followed by a decrease in demand

options.label: E
options.text: A decrease in the good's own price followed by a decrease in demand

explanation: A to B raises purchases at the same price by shifting demand right. B to C then lowers price along D2 and increases quantity demanded.

prompt: A consumer is willing to pay $18 for a fourth unit and $14 for a fifth unit. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The marginal benefit of the fifth unit is $14 and is lower than that of the fourth

options.label: B
options.text: The consumer's market demand is $18 at four units and $32 at five units because willingness to pay is added vertically

options.label: C
options.text: The decline in willingness to pay shows that demand shifted left between units

options.label: D
options.text: The marginal benefit of the fifth unit is $32 because willingness to pay is cumulative

options.label: E
options.text: The marginal benefit of the fourth unit is $14 and rises for the fifth unit

explanation: The fifth unit's $14 willingness to pay is its marginal benefit. It is $4 below the fourth unit's $18 benefit.

prompt: Which of the following best explains why a consumer may buy a second slice of pizza only at a lower price than the first?

options.label: A
options.text: The second slice increases the consumer's nominal income less than the first

options.label: B
options.text: The second slice shifts the consumer's demand curve farther to the right

options.label: C
options.text: The first slice adds another buyer to the market demand curve

options.label: D
options.text: The second slice provides less marginal utility than the first slice

options.label: E
options.text: The first slice creates a legal constraint that applies to later slices

explanation: The second slice adds less satisfaction than the first. A lower price is therefore needed to make that additional slice worth buying.

prompt: A 20 percent decrease in the price of a frequently purchased good causes a consumer to buy more of it. Which two mechanisms can both contribute to this response?

options.label: A
options.text: The substitution effect and the increase in real purchasing power

options.label: B
options.text: The substitution effect and a decrease in real purchasing power

options.label: C
options.text: Diminishing marginal utility and a decrease in nominal income

options.label: D
options.text: A larger number of buyers and an increase in nominal income

options.label: E
options.text: A rightward demand shift and a smaller number of alternatives

explanation: The lower price makes the good more attractive relative to substitutes. It also lets the same income purchase more, increasing real purchasing power.

prompt: At a price of $5, three buyers demand 8, 6, and 4 units. One buyer's demand then rises from 6 to 9 units at that price. What happens to market quantity demanded?

options.label: A
options.text: It increases from 18 units to 21 units

options.label: B
options.text: It decreases from 18 units to 15 units

options.label: C
options.text: It remains at 18 units because only one buyer changed

options.label: D
options.text: It increases from 14 units to 17 units

options.label: E
options.text: It increases from 18 units to 24 units

explanation: Initial purchases total 8 + 6 + 4 = 18 units. The buyer's extra 3 units raise market quantity to 21.

explanation: Underage consumers leave the market at all prices after the regulation. Their removal reduces market demand rather than creating a price-driven movement along the curve.

prompt: A shopper values two stores equally but chooses the closer one after the available shopping time falls from one hour to twenty minutes. This change shows that

options.label: B
options.text: A shorter trip creates a movement along the product's demand curve

options.label: C
options.text: Unchanged preferences require the shopper to make the same choice

options.label: D
options.text: A tighter time constraint can alter the choice even when preferences are unchanged

options.label: E
options.text: A tighter time constraint must reduce the shopper's nominal income before any purchase choice can change

explanation: Less shopping time makes the farther store harder to use. The consumer can change stores because feasible choices change even when preferences stay the same.

prompt: Which of the following would most directly weaken a buyer's incentive to participate in a market for used electronics?

options.label: A
options.text: Clear records showing that sellers own the devices they offer

options.label: B
options.text: A larger number of buyers included in the market demand schedule

options.label: C
options.text: A higher expected future price for comparable electronic devices

options.label: D
options.text: Uncertainty about whether sellers have the right to transfer ownership

options.label: E
options.text: A lower current price for the device the buyer is considering

explanation: If the seller cannot securely transfer ownership, the buyer risks losing control of the purchase. That uncertainty weakens the incentive to buy.

prompt: Based on the figure below, which conclusion is valid?

options.label: A
options.text: Quantity demanded increased because the good's own price fell from P1 to P2

options.label: B
options.text: Demand rises at both prices, not necessarily equally

options.label: E
options.text: Quantity demanded remained unchanged because both curves slope downward

explanation: D2 is farther right at both P1 and P2, so demand is higher at each price. The horizontal gaps can differ because demand shifts need not be parallel.

prompt: Demand for a normal good increases when income rises. Which additional change would reinforce that increase?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: A decrease in the price of a substitute

options.label: C
options.text: An increase in the number of buyers

options.label: D
options.text: An expectation that the good's future price will fall

options.label: E
options.text: A decrease in the number of buyers

explanation: More buyers add purchases to market demand at every price. This reinforces the increase caused by higher income for a normal good.

prompt: Consumer income rises for a normal good while the price of a substitute falls. What can be concluded about demand for the good?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand must increase because both determinants shift it to the right

options.label: B
options.text: Quantity demanded must decrease along the original demand curve

options.label: C
options.text: The direction is indeterminate because the two determinants have opposing effects

options.label: D
options.text: Quantity demanded must increase because the own-price is unchanged

options.label: E
options.text: Demand must decrease because both determinants shift it to the left

explanation: Higher income raises demand for the normal good, but a cheaper substitute draws buyers away. Their relative effects are needed to determine the net shift.

prompt: Consumers develop a stronger preference for a good at the same time its own price rises. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Both changes cause rightward shifts because each increases willingness to buy

options.label: B
options.text: Demand shifts left, while the higher price causes movement downward along the new curve

options.label: C
options.text: Demand shifts right, while the higher price causes movement upward along the new curve

options.label: D
options.text: Demand remains fixed because preferences and price are changing simultaneously

options.label: E
options.text: Both changes cause movement because each changes the quantity purchased

explanation: Greater preference shifts demand right. The higher price then moves the chosen quantity up and left along that new curve.

prompt: Income rises by the same amount for two consumers. Demand for Good A rises while demand for Good B falls. Which classification is supported?

options.label: A
options.text: Goods A and B are substitutes because their demands move oppositely

options.label: B
options.text: Both goods are normal because the consumers' nominal income increased

options.label: C
options.text: Good A is inferior and Good B is normal for these consumers

options.label: D
options.text: Good A is normal and Good B is inferior for these consumers

options.label: E
options.text: Goods A and B are complements because their demands move oppositely

explanation: Good A's demand rises with income, making it normal. Good B's demand falls with income, making it inferior for these consumers.

prompt: Based on the figures below, which statement correctly compares the effects of the same income increase?

options.label: D
options.text: Demand for both goods shifts right because purchasing power increased

options.label: E

explanation: Income increases purchases of the normal good at each price and reduces purchases of the inferior good. Their demand curves shift right and left, respectively.

prompt: A product's current price is unchanged, but consumers expect it to become scarce and more expensive next month. Which observation is most consistent with the law of demand and the expectations effect?

prompt: Two consumers place the same value on a gym membership, but only one has sufficient income and time to attend. Which statement best explains their different purchase decisions?

options.text: Different time constraints cause movement along a shared market demand curve

options.text: Effective demand depends on ability to purchase and relevant constraints, not preference alone

prompt: At a price of $10, four consumers demand 6, 5, 4, and 3 units. The consumer demanding 5 units exits the market, while each remaining consumer increases demand by 2 units at that price. What is the new market quantity demanded?

options.label: B
options.text: 13 units

options.label: C
options.text: 24 units

options.label: D
options.text: 21 units

options.label: E
options.text: 19 units

explanation: Removing the 5-unit buyer leaves 6 + 4 + 3 = 13 units. Three remaining buyers each add 2, giving 13 + 6 = 19 units.

prompt: At a price of $15, buyers A, B, and C demand 4, 0, and 3 units. At a price of $12, they demand 6, 2, and 5 units. Which statement correctly describes market demand?

options.label: A
options.text: Market quantity rises from 4 to 6 units because only buyer A purchases at both prices

explanation: At $15, market demand totals 4 + 0 + 3 = 7 units. At $12, it totals 6 + 2 + 5 = 13, including B's 2 units.

prompt: Demand for a normal good is affected by a rise in income, a fall in the price of a substitute, and an expected increase in the good's future price. Which conclusion is valid?

options.text: Quantity demanded must rise because the good's current price is unchanged

prompt: At every price, a decrease in the price of a complement adds 6 units to demand for Good X, while the exit of several buyers removes 4 units. Which change occurs in market demand for Good X?

options.text: It increases by 2 units at each price

options.label: E
options.text: It decreases by 10 units at each price

prompt: At a price of $20, three original buyers demand 5, 7, and 4 units. A fourth buyer enters demanding 6 units, while each original buyer reduces demand by 1 unit. What is the new market quantity demanded at $20?

options.text: 22 units

options.text: 13 units

prompt: At a price of $8, market quantity demanded is 30 units. Buyer A demands 12 units, and Buyer B demands twice as many units as Buyer C. If these are the only buyers, how many units does Buyer B demand?

prompt: The price of tea rises, demand for coffee rises, and demand for cream also rises. Which set of relationships is consistent with these observations, ceteris paribus?

options.text: Coffee is inferior, while tea and cream must both be normal goods

options.text: Tea and coffee are complements, while tea and cream must be complements

options.label: D
options.text: Tea and coffee are substitutes, while coffee and cream are complements

options.label: E
options.text: Tea and coffee are complements, while coffee and cream are substitutes

explanation: A higher tea price encourages buyers to substitute coffee. More coffee purchases also raise cream demand when coffee and cream are consumed together.

prompt: Income rises for a normal good, but consumers also expect the good's price to fall next month. Which information is needed to predict the change in current demand?

options.label: A
options.text: The relative sizes of the rightward income effect and leftward expectations effect

options.label: B
options.text: The marginal utility from only the first unit purchased by each consumer

options.label: C
options.text: The average rather than total quantity demanded by current consumers

options.label: D
options.text: The size of the good's current price change along the original demand curve

options.label: E
options.text: The nominal income level without knowing how income affects this normal good

explanation: Higher income encourages current purchases, while expected lower future prices encourage waiting. The larger of these opposing effects determines the net change.

prompt: A good's price falls while an unrelated change shifts its demand curve left. What can be concluded about the final quantity purchased compared with the initial quantity?

options.label: A
options.text: It must decrease because a leftward demand shift always lowers the final quantity purchased

options.label: B
options.text: It equals the original quantity because own-price changes cannot accompany demand shifts

options.text: It remains unchanged because a movement and a shift always offset exactly

options.text: It must increase because a lower own-price always raises the final quantity purchased

options.label: E

explanation: A lower price encourages more purchases, but lower demand discourages them. Their relative sizes determine whether final purchases rise or fall.

prompt: Researchers observe that a good's price and quantity purchased both increased between two months. Why does this observation not disprove the law of demand?

options.label: A
options.text: The law of demand applies only when consumer income changes between observations

options.label: B
options.text: The law of demand predicts that price and quantity always rise together over time

options.label: C
options.text: Market demand is found by vertically adding individual prices between observations

options.label: D
options.text: A higher price shifts the demand curve right and raises the quantity purchased

options.label: E
options.text: A demand determinant may have shifted the demand curve between the observations

explanation: The law of demand assumes other determinants remain constant. A rightward demand shift can produce observations with both a higher price and more purchases.

options.label: E

prompt: A consumer's demand curve shows willingness to pay of $30, $22, $16, and $11 for successive units. If the price falls from $20 to $12, which change occurs?

options.label: E

prompt: Unverified property claims make buyers reluctant to purchase land even when listed prices fall. Which explanation best accounts for this behavior?

options.label: A
options.text: The lower price shifts land demand right, and insecure rights cause movement back along that curve

options.label: B
options.text: The lower price reduces real purchasing power, while insecure rights increase marginal utility

options.label: C
options.text: The lower price creates an incentive to buy, but insecure property rights remain a constraint on exchange

options.label: D
options.text: The lower price eliminates income constraints, so property rights cannot affect demand

options.label: E
options.text: The lower price adds buyers to market demand, while insecure rights change horizontal summation

explanation: A lower price encourages buying, but uncertain ownership makes the transaction risky. Insecure property rights can therefore continue to discourage purchases.

prompt: For an ordinary good, a decrease in its own price increases quantity demanded through both the substitution and income effects because

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: Marginal utility rises for successive units and the consumer postpones purchases

options.label: E
options.text: The good becomes relatively more expensive and the consumer's real purchasing power falls

explanation: The lower price makes the good cheaper than alternatives and raises the purchasing power of unchanged income. For the ordinary good described, these effects support increased quantity demanded.

prompt: Income increases for both a normal good and an inferior good while each good's own price decreases. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Purchases of the normal good rise, but the change in purchases of the inferior good is indeterminate

options.label: B
options.text: Purchases of both goods must rise because both demand curves shift right

options.label: C
options.text: Purchases of the normal good are indeterminate, but purchases of the inferior good rise

options.label: D
options.text: Purchases of both goods must fall because both own-prices decrease

options.label: E
options.text: Purchases of the normal good fall, while purchases of the inferior good are unchanged

explanation: For the normal good, higher income and a lower price both raise purchases. For the inferior good, the income-driven demand decrease opposes the price-driven increase, leaving the net effect uncertain.

prompt: The price of Good Y increases, and the demand curve for Good X shifts right. If all other demand determinants for X are unchanged, which conclusion is supported?

options.label: E
options.text: Goods X and Y are complements

prompt: Which combination of changes will unambiguously decrease current demand for a normal good?

options.label: A
options.text: Income rises, a complement's price falls, and consumers expect the future price to fall

options.label: B
options.text: Income rises, a substitute's price falls, and consumers expect the future price to rise

options.label: D
options.text: Income falls, a substitute's price rises, and the number of buyers increases

options.label: E
options.text: Income falls, a substitute's price falls, and consumers expect the good's future price to fall

explanation: Lower income reduces demand for a normal good, and a cheaper substitute attracts buyers away. Expected future price decreases also encourage waiting, so all three changes reduce current demand.

prompt: After several buyers enter and others leave a market, the total quantity demanded at every listed price is unchanged. Which conclusion is supported?

options.label: A
options.text: The good's own price must have changed by the same amount at every listed quantity

options.label: B
options.text: Every individual demand curve must be unchanged because market totals are unchanged

options.label: C
options.text: Market demand is unchanged even though the composition and individual demands may have changed

options.label: D
options.text: Market demand shifted right and then moved left along the new demand curve

options.label: E
options.text: The entrants and exiting buyers must demand identical quantities at every price

explanation: Market demand adds individual purchases at each price. Changes in who buys can leave those totals, and therefore the market demand curve, unchanged.
